summary:
We built AstroNOTok, a health monitoring tool for astronauts. Stand in front of a laptop camera, and a transparent 3D body overlays onto you, colour-coded green, yellow or red by how each part of you is doing. Point and hold to see what is going on. Rotate the model with an open hand, close a panel with a fist.

No typing, no tapping a screen. Why? In microgravity, astronauts float. Their hands are gloved, gripping a rail, or busy. Pressing a keyboard literally pushes you away from it. So we designed every interaction to work with gestures and camera alone.

What makes this different is how we define normal. The body changes in space. Blood pressure drops, temperature rises, sleep shifts. A reading that looks alarming on Earth might be completely expected mid-mission. So instead of fixed thresholds, we compare each astronaut to their own pre-flight baseline, adjusted for known spaceflight changes and mission day. Normal adaptation does not trigger false alarms. Real problems show up early.

We use real NASA data (ISS radiation, cabin air telemetry and Inspiration4 crew blood tests). We also used Arduino and PulseSensor to stream live heart rate into the app, and the 3D heart actually beats in sync with the user’s pulse.

But none of it matters if astronauts do not open the app. So we added exercises with on-camera rep counting, daily check-ins, and 3D companions they can pet and feed. On a long mission with no doctor, staying engaged with your health is half the battle.
details:
What AstroNOTok does

Astronauts have access to a lot of health data during space missions. But having the data is one thing, understanding what it means and knowing what to do about it is another. Especially when you are millions of kilometres away from Earth and cannot simply walk into a clinic.

That is the problem we want to solve with AstroNOTok. We want to make health monitoring something astronauts can understand and act on themselves, without needing a medical background.

Instead of showing astronauts a dashboard full of numbers and medical terms, we built a 3D human body that overlays onto their live camera feed. They can actually see their own skeleton, organs, and beating heart, with different body regions coloured according to their health status. If something needs attention, a red indicator appears right next to that body part.

We also thought about how astronauts would interact with the application. In space, using a mouse or keyboard might not always be practical, especially when they are wearing gloves or working in zero gravity. So we made the interface touch-free. Astronauts can point and hold to select a body part, rotate the model with an open hand, and close a panel by making a fist.

But the most important part is what happens after they open a health reading. We don't want astronauts to have to interpret complicated medical terminology. Instead of just showing "70 bpm", we explain that their heart rate is 70 bpm when it is usually around 55, and tell them what they can do next. It could be something as simple as doing 12 squats, or speaking to their medical officer if the reading is concerning.

The idea is to translate health data into something genuinely useful, while still keeping the technical details available for the medical officer to review.

How we make health monitoring more accurate

One of the biggest challenges we identified was deciding what actually counts as an abnormal health reading in space.

The human body changes naturally in microgravity. Blood pressure can decrease, body temperature can rise, and heart rate can shift over the course of a mission. If we simply applied the same health thresholds that we use on Earth, we might end up flagging perfectly normal adaptations as medical problems.

So instead of comparing every astronaut against the same population average, we compare them against themselves.

We start with each astronaut's pre-flight health baseline, then adjust what we expect to see based on their mission day and published research on physiological changes in space. For example, our model accounts for an approximately 8 mmHg reduction in blood pressure and a 1°C increase in core temperature. We also retain fixed safety limits, because some readings are dangerous regardless of whether they are expected.

This means that a slightly elevated heart rate in the first month of a mission would not automatically trigger a warning if it follows the expected adaptation pattern. What concerns us is when the astronaut starts deviating from their own expected trajectory, especially when several health indicators begin changing together.

I think this is an important distinction. We are not just trying to detect unusual numbers. We are trying to understand whether those numbers are unusual for that particular person, at that particular point in their mission.

Making astronauts actually want to use it

Another thing we thought about was engagement. Even if we built a really accurate monitoring system, it would not be very useful if astronauts stopped checking it after a few days.

And on long missions to the Moon or Mars, physical health is only part of the picture. Astronauts also have to deal with stress, isolation, and being away from their families for months or even years.

So we wanted to make AstroNOTok something astronauts would actually look forward to using.

Every day, astronauts can complete a quick mood and stress check-in. Based on their health readings, the application can also recommend simple exercises, such as squats, arm raises, or knee lifts. The camera tracks their movements and automatically counts their repetitions, so they don't need any additional equipment. We also included a guided box-breathing exercise to help them manage stress.

And this is where we added something a little more fun.

Astronauts earn points by completing their daily check-ins and exercises. They can then use those points to adopt 3D animal companions, which they can pet, feed, pick up, and play with.

It might sound a little silly to have virtual pets in a medical application, but there is a reason behind it. We wanted to give astronauts a simple way to stay engaged with their daily health routine, especially during long periods of isolation. The companions also give them a small motivation to return to the application every day. 

Rather than treating health monitoring as another task astronauts have to complete, we want it to become a positive part of their daily routine.

Connecting the software to real health sensors

We integrated a wearable pulse sensor controlled by arduino that can stream live heart-rate data into the application. From the pulse waveform, we can also estimate indicators such as heart-rate variability and breathing rate.

One of my favourite details is that the 3D heart actually beats according to the astronaut's real pulse. So when their heart rate increases, they can see it reflected immediately in the model.

We also designed the system so that when the physical sensor is disconnected, the application can switch back to simulated data. This allows us to demonstrate and test the full experience even without having access to all the medical equipment used aboard a space station.

How we built it

The biggest technical challenge was that we obviously do not have access to an actual space station or all of NASA's medical monitoring devices.

So we decided to simulate the environment as realistically as we could, while keeping the system flexible enough to connect to real devices in the future.

Our Flask backend simulates health readings from equipment such as the Bio-Monitor smart shirt, Actiwatch, Thermo-Mini, Tempus Pro, rHEALTH One, portable ultrasound devices, and exercise equipment. We designed these simulators to follow the same data structures and timing patterns that real hardware adapters would use.

We also wanted to ground the simulation in actual spaceflight conditions instead of making everything up.

For radiation exposure, we replay NASA's DOSTEL measurements from RadLab, including data from the May 2024 solar particle event. For environmental conditions, we use NASA's Open Science Data Repository to reproduce changes in cabin CO₂, temperature, and humidity.

To make the demonstration more interesting, we accelerated the mission clock by 60 times. This allows us to show how an astronaut's health might change over time without having to wait through an entire mission.

Behind the interface, we built a health engine that takes all these readings, compares them against the astronaut's expected health trajectory, and determines which body regions need attention. It then translates those findings into something actionable, whether that means an exercise recommendation, a simple health precaution, or a referral to the crew medical officer.

On the frontend, we use MediaPipe for body and hand tracking, and Three.js to render the interactive 3D body.

One design decision we made early on was that the core application should work completely offline. On Earth, we are used to applications that depend on cloud services and constant internet access. But on a mission to Mars, communication with Earth can be significantly delayed. We cannot build a tool that depends on an immediate response from a remote server whenever an astronaut wants to check their health.

So our application is designed to run locally on a single laptop, without requiring an internet connection.

What we hope to achieve

Ultimately, we are not trying to replace medical officers or build a system that diagnoses astronauts on its own.

What we want to build is a tool that makes astronauts more aware of their own health and helps them take small, meaningful actions before minor issues become serious problems.

I think the most exciting part of AstroNOTok is that we are bringing together several ideas that are usually treated separately: personalised health monitoring, augmented reality, human-computer interaction, and behavioural engagement.

The technology itself is interesting, but what matters more is whether an astronaut can open the application, understand what is happening to their body, and know what to do next.

Right now, we are using simulated space station devices alongside a real pulse sensor. But because we designed the backend with interchangeable data sources, the simulators could eventually be replaced with connections to actual medical equipment without having to rebuild the rest of the application.

Our goal is to create something that could eventually support astronauts on long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars, where being able to understand and manage your own health is not just convenient, but increasingly important.

Tools and technologies

Backend: Python, Flask, NumPy, SQLite, pyserial

Frontend: JavaScript, HTML/CSS, Three.js, MediaPipe Tasks Vision (pose, hand, and face tracking)

Hardware: Arduino, PulseSensor

Data sources: NASA RadLab, NASA Open Science Data Repository

Development tools: GitHub, Vercel
